To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

glutamine synthetases of tumors are usually inactive, but that the activity of glutamine in serum and tissues of tumor-bearing animals is maintained at normal or near-normal levels by the action of the liver.

glutamine synthetases in liver of rats bearing hepatomas, and the γ-glutamylepeptidases in liver and kidney of these rats, are not as different from the enzymes of normal rat liver as are the glutamyl-RNAs synthetases of these tumors and of the livers of rats bearing them.
In summary, our research is concerned with
enzymes related to glutamine metabolism in the normal and tumor-bearing rat.
the role of glutamine in tumor metabolism.
the metabolic changes that take place in the host when he bears a tumor.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
glutamine metabolism in tumors is altered in a manner that is not yet understood, but that it is not altered in a single, uniform manner.

glutamine synthetases in tumors are not necessarily abnormal, but that the enzyme in tumors may be either normal or abnormal, and that glutamyl- or glutaminyl-RNAs synthetase activities may be normal, low or high, and γ-gluta-myltranspeptidine activities may be normal or low.

the metabolism of glutamine in tumors is not significantly different from that in normal tissues, but that the metabolism of this amino acid in the liver of the host of a slow growing tumor may be different from that in the liver or normal rats.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, with the possible exception of Morris hepatomas, the enzymes of glutamine metabolism are not maintained in normal amounts in the host9s tissues, nor do tumors possess normal activities of these enzymes.
, although the activities of glutamine synthase, glutaminy-RNA synthetases, and γ-glutanyltranspeptidas in Morris hepatoma are not normal, they are not as low as in other hepatomas.

the activities of glutamine synthase and γ-glutamiltranspeptidases in tumors and in tissues of the hosts are of little value as criteria for the classification of hepatomas, but that the activities of these enzymes in tumors may be of value in determining the degree of deviation of the tumor from normal liver.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the enzymes of glutamine metabolism, which have been shown in the past to be of importance in the growth of normal tissues, are also of importance in the metabolism of the host in relation to the growth of tumors.
the liver and brain of the rat bearing Morris hepatoma are able to maintain normal levels of free glutamine, even though the liver is not able to maintain normal glutaminase activity.
glutamine synthetases, glutaminyl-RNAs synthetases, and γ-gluta-mytranspeptidases of tumors and of normal liver differ markedly in their properties.
